Name: Norse Paganism
Description: Pre-Christian polytheistic religion of the Norse people, emphasizing honor, fate, and the cosmic struggle between order and chaos.
CreationMyth: In the beginning was Ginnungagap, the void between fire (Muspelheim) and ice (Niflheim). When fire and ice met, the giant Ymir was born from the melting ice. The first god, Búri, emerged from ice licked by the cow Auðumbla. Búri's grandsons—Odin, Vili, and Vé—slew Ymir and created the world from his body: his flesh became earth, his blood the seas, his bones the mountains, his hair the trees, and his skull the sky. From two tree trunks they created the first humans, Ask and Embla, giving them breath, consciousness, and form. The gods built Asgard in the sky, connected to Midgard (the human world) by the rainbow bridge Bifröst.
CorePrinciples: Honor and reputation (frith) paramount
Fate (wyrd) is inescapable, even for gods
Courage in face of inevitable doom (Ragnarök)
Reciprocity and gift-giving build relationships
Strength and martial prowess valued
Connection to ancestors and land
Nine worlds connected by Yggdrasil, the World Tree
NotableFigures: Odin (All-Father, god of wisdom and war)

Name: Ancient Greek Religion
Description: Polytheistic religion of ancient Greece centered on the Olympian gods, emphasizing ritual, sacrifice, and human excellence.
CreationMyth: In the beginning was Chaos, the void. From Chaos emerged Gaia (Earth), Tartarus (the underworld), and Eros (love). Gaia gave birth to Ouranos (Sky), and together they produced the Titans. The Titan Kronos overthrew Ouranos, then swallowed his own children to prevent being overthrown. Zeus, hidden by his mother Rhea, escaped and led the Olympian gods in a ten-year war (Titanomachy) against the Titans. Zeus and his siblings—Poseidon, Hades, Hera, Demeter, and Hestia—defeated the Titans and established rule from Mount Olympus. Prometheus shaped humans from clay, and Athena breathed life into them. Zeus punished Prometheus for giving fire to humans by chaining him to a rock.
CorePrinciples: Hubris (excessive pride) leads to nemesis (downfall)
Honor the gods through ritual and sacrifice
Arete: excellence and virtue in all endeavors
Fate (moira) governs all, even gods
Hospitality (xenia) is sacred
Know thyself (Delphic maxim)
Nothing in excess (Delphic maxim)

Name: Ancient Egyptian Religion
Description: Complex polytheistic religion emphasizing the afterlife, cosmic order (ma'at), and the divine pharaoh.
Sources: Book of the Dead (Book of Coming Forth by Day)
CreationMyth: In the beginning was Nun, the primordial waters of chaos. From Nun emerged the benben, the primordial mound, upon which the creator god Atum appeared. Atum was alone and complete in himself. Through his own power, he created Shu (air) and Tefnut (moisture), who in turn gave birth to Geb (earth) and Nut (sky). From Geb and Nut came Osiris, Isis, Set, and Nephthys. Atum/Ra became the sun god, traveling across the sky by day in his solar barque and through the underworld (Duat) by night, battling the chaos serpent Apophis to ensure the sun would rise again. Humans were created from the tears of Ra.
CorePrinciples: Ma'at: cosmic order, truth, justice, and balance
Afterlife more important than earthly life
Pharaoh is divine intermediary between gods and humans
Heart weighed against feather of Ma'at in judgment
Preservation of body (mummification) for afterlife
Ka (life force), ba (personality), akh (spirit) survive death
Cyclical time: death and rebirth like daily sun

Name: Mesopotamian Religion (Sumerian/Babylonian)
Description: Polytheistic religion of ancient Mesopotamia emphasizing service to capricious gods and acceptance of human limitations.
CreationMyth: In the beginning, only Apsu (fresh water) and Tiamat (salt water) existed, their waters mingling. From their union came the first gods, whose noise disturbed Apsu. He planned to destroy them, but the god Ea killed Apsu first. Tiamat, enraged, created monsters and chose Kingu as her champion. The young god Marduk agreed to fight Tiamat if the other gods made him supreme king. He defeated Tiamat, split her body in half to create heaven and earth, and used Kingu's blood to create humans. Humans were created as servants to the gods, to feed them through sacrifice and relieve them of labor. The gods built the city of Babylon and the great ziggurat Etemenanki as Marduk's dwelling place.
CorePrinciples: Humans created to serve the gods
Gods are powerful but capricious and petty
Fate is controlled by divine council, not individual will
Death is final; underworld is gloomy shadow existence
Cities and temples are centers of divine presence
Kings rule by divine mandate
Accept human mortality and limitations

Name: Aztec Religion
Description: Complex polytheistic religion emphasizing cosmic cycles, human sacrifice to maintain universal order, and the dual nature of existence.
Sources: Historia de las Indias de Nueva España (Diego Durán)
CreationMyth: The world has been created and destroyed four times before the current era (the Fifth Sun). In the beginning, the dual god Ometeotl divided into male and female aspects, creating the four Tezcatlipocas and Quetzalcoatl. These gods created the earth from the body of the earth monster Cipactli. Four previous worlds (suns) were each destroyed by jaguars, wind, fire, and flood. The current Fifth Sun was created at Teotihuacan when the gods sacrificed themselves, and the humble god Nanahuatzin threw himself into a fire to become the sun. But the sun wouldn't move until the other gods sacrificed their blood. Quetzalcoatl descended to the underworld (Mictlan) and retrieved the bones of previous humans, sprinkling them with his own blood to create humanity. Humans must maintain the sun through blood sacrifice.
CorePrinciples: Blood sacrifice necessary to maintain cosmic order
Duality: life/death, order/chaos in constant balance
Current world (Fifth Sun) will inevitably end
Humans created to nourish gods with blood
Warfare to capture sacrificial victims (Flower Wars)
Calendrical precision: 260-day ritual and 365-day solar
Warrior's death or childbirth death grants paradise
NotableFigures: Quetzalcoatl (feathered serpent, god of wind and learning)

Name: Yoruba Religion
Description: Traditional religion of the Yoruba people emphasizing a supreme creator, intermediary orishas, and ancestor veneration.
CreationMyth: In the beginning, there was only Olodumare, the supreme creator, and the primordial waters below the sky. Olodumare sent the orisha Obatala down with a chain, a snail shell with sand, and a chicken to create land. But Obatala drank palm wine and fell asleep, so Olodumare sent Oduduwa instead to spread the sand and let the chicken scratch it to create the first land at Ile-Ife, the sacred city. Obatala later molded humans from clay, but when he drank palm wine while working, he created people with disabilities; afterward, he became their protector. Olodumare breathed life into the clay forms. The orishas are divine forces of nature and human experience, intermediaries between Olodumare and humanity. Each person has a destiny (ori) chosen before birth.
CorePrinciples: Olodumare is supreme, distant creator
Orishas as intermediaries: forces of nature and archetypes
Ancestor veneration maintains family lineage
Divination (Ifá) reveals destiny and guidance
Ashe: spiritual power/life force in all things
Each person has ori (destiny/inner head)
Balance between opposing forces
